patient.name: Daniel Osei
patient.complaint: Painful swollen right upper arm and cannot lift his right wrist after a cycling fall
background: Fell off his bike onto his right arm in Hackney

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which nerve is most likely injured?' or 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a mechanism (fracture, crutches, sleeping on an arm, birth) plus a motor sign (wrist drop, claw hand, foot drop, waiter's tip) and a sensory patch.

points: Daniel, 27, fell from his bike onto his outstretched right arm.
He **cannot lift his right wrist** or straighten his fingers.
Numb patch on the back of his hand near the thumb.

steps.lead: Daniel has a **trauma** cause and a clear **motor deficit**: the motor loss is what tells you which nerve is hurt.

steps.q: Daniel has a mid-shaft humeral fracture and wrist drop. Which nerve is injured?
steps.r: The **radial nerve** runs in the spiral groove of the humerus and is the nerve most often injured in **mid-shaft humeral fractures**.

visual.title: Daniel's wrist extension (MRC power)
visual.label: Daniel 1/5
visual.caption: A flicker only: **wrist drop**. Elbow extension (triceps) is 5/5, so the lesion is below the triceps branches.

steps.lead: Daniel's triceps works, so this is not a high (axillary, crutch) lesion: it is at the **humeral shaft**.

steps.title: Which nerve? Motor sign and sensory loss
head: Nerve
Typical cause
Motor sign
Sensory loss

steps.lead: Same nerve, different story: if Daniel had slept drunk with his arm over a chair, this would be **Saturday night palsy**.

steps.text: Level decides the sign: **humeral shaft** radial lesion gives **wrist drop**; a lesion at the elbow (posterior interosseous) gives **finger drop with intact sensation**.
Foot drop with weak **inversion as well as eversion** is an **L5 root** lesion, not common peroneal palsy. Peroneal palsy spares inversion (tibial nerve).

steps.lead: Daniel's picture is a single peripheral nerve. The list below holds the look-alikes the exam pairs with nerve palsies: roots, cranial nerves and neuropathies.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?' where the answer is usually clinical examination, or nerve conduction studies when the site or the diagnosis is unclear; in GBS, FVC monitors breathing.

points: X-ray: transverse **mid-shaft fracture of the right humerus**.
Radial pulse present; hand warm, capillary refill under 2 seconds.
Wrist and finger extensors weak; triceps, biceps and grip normal.

steps.q: What confirms Daniel's radial nerve palsy?
steps.r: **Clinical examination** is the gold standard: the motor and sensory pattern localises the nerve.

steps.lead: Daniel's examination localises the lesion. **Nerve conduction studies and EMG** are kept for when recovery stalls or the site is unclear.

steps.title: Daniel's nerve conduction study at 6 weeks
steps.text: Conduction block with preserved axons below the lesion: **neurapraxia**, the best prognosis.

steps.title: Localising a nerve lesion
nodes: Map to one nerve, root or plexus
Unclear or not recovering → NCS / EMG

steps.text: Do not reach for imaging to diagnose a nerve palsy. **Examination** finds the nerve; NCS/EMG confirms and grades it if needed.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': treat the cause (fracture, cast, compression), splint and physiotherapy; carpal tunnel is splint with or without steroid injection, then flexor retinaculum release; GBS is IV immunoglobulin.

steps.lead: Daniel has a fracture with a nerve injury, so the first job is an urgent **neurovascular** check of the arm.

steps.q: Daniel's hand is warm with a radial pulse. What is the best initial plan?
o: Splint the fracture and the wrist, then physiotherapy
steps.r: Treat the **fracture**, support the wrist in a **splint** and start **physiotherapy**. Most closed-fracture radial palsies are neurapraxias that recover.

steps.lead: Daniel's fracture is managed, and a **wrist splint** keeps his hand functional while the nerve recovers.

visual.title: Daniel's recovery of wrist extension
visual.caption: Recovering by 8 weeks: a **neurapraxia**. No recovery by 3 to 4 months would prompt NCS and surgical exploration.

steps.title: Peripheral nerve injury: management ladder
nodes: Treat the cause: fracture, remove compression

steps.lead: Not Daniel's nerve, but the exam favourite: **carpal tunnel** gets a splint first, surgery second; **GBS** gets **IV immunoglobulin**.

steps.title: Carpal tunnel syndrome: step by step
head: Situation
Treatment
rows: Surgical division of the flexor retinaculum

steps.lead: Carpal tunnel follows **NICE CKS**; suspected GBS follows **NICE NG157** (urgent same-day assessment).

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the Seddon grade and prognosis, why compression causes weakness without transection, molecular mimicry in GBS, or the inheritance of Charcot-Marie-Tooth.

visual.title: Seddon classification
visual.label: Daniel: neurapraxia
visual.caption: Daniel's quick recovery places him at the best-prognosis end.

steps.lead: Daniel recovered in weeks, so his nerve was stretched and bruised, a **neurapraxia**, not cut.
In compression palsies the nerve is intact: focal **demyelination and ischaemia** block conduction, so it can recover once pressure is off.

steps.q: Which Seddon grade needs surgical repair?
steps.r: **Neurotmesis** is complete transection: the worst prognosis and needs repair. Axonotmesis regrows along the intact endoneurium.

steps.lead: Unlike Daniel's mechanical injury, **GBS** is immune: antibodies to *Campylobacter* cross-react with nerve **gangliosides**.
Charcot-Marie-Tooth is a lifelong, **inherited** cause of foot drop, very different from Daniel's sudden traumatic one.
A purely **sensory** nerve trapped under the inguinal ligament gives burning thigh pain but, unlike Daniel, no weakness.

mcq.q: Which nerve is most commonly injured in a mid-shaft humeral fracture?
mcq.r: The **radial nerve** lies in the spiral groove: wrist drop.

mcq.q: Which finding fits carpal tunnel syndrome?
mcq.r: Median nerve at the wrist: weak **APB** and **thenar** (not hypothenar) wasting.

mcq.q: What posture is seen in Erb's palsy?
mcq.r: **C5/C6**: adducted, internally rotated arm, extended forearm, flexed wrist.

mcq.q: Which is the triad of Miller Fisher syndrome?
mcq.r: A **GBS variant** starting with the eyes; linked to Campylobacter.

mcq.q: Foot drop with weak eversion but normal inversion suggests a lesion of which nerve?
mcq.r: **Common peroneal**; loss of inversion as well points to **L5**.

mcq.q: What is the gold standard for diagnosing a peripheral nerve palsy?
mcq.r: **Clinical examination**; NCS/EMG if needed to localise or confirm.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment for mild carpal tunnel syndrome in pregnancy?
mcq.r: **Splint ± steroid injection**; often settles after delivery.

mcq.q: Which structure is divided in carpal tunnel surgery?
mcq.r: Dividing the **flexor retinaculum** decompresses the median nerve.

mcq.q: What is first-line treatment for Guillain-Barré syndrome?
mcq.r: **IVIG** plus supportive care; steroids are not used.

mcq.q: Which Seddon class has the best prognosis?

technique.stem: A 58 year old man fell onto his left elbow 3 months ago. He now has weakness of his left hand and numbness of his little finger. His 4th and 5th fingers are clawed. He cannot spread his fingers apart, and on resisted wrist flexion the wrist deviates radially.
technique.q: Which nerve is most likely injured?
o: Radial nerve at the spiral groove

steps.x: Which nerve, and at what level: use the motor sign and the sensory patch.
Claw of 4th and 5th digits, weak finger abduction, little-finger numbness, and loss of **FCU** (radial deviation).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ulnar nerve** injury at the **elbow** (FCU involved).

elim: Pure motor; weak pinch (thumb and index flexion), no clawing.
Thenar wasting and lateral finger numbness.
Wrist drop with dorsal web space numbness.

steps.x: **E. Ulnar nerve at the elbow.** Claw hand + lost FCU = ulnar at the elbow.

technique.stem: A 30 year old man has had a weak left wrist since waking on a park bench after a night of heavy drinking 2 days ago. He cannot extend his wrist or fingers. Sensation is reduced over the back of the hand near the thumb. Triceps power is normal. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

steps.x: Confirm the diagnosis: name it, then its gold standard.

clues: cannot extend his wrist or fingers
back of the hand near the thumb
steps.x: Typical **Saturday night palsy**: radial nerve compressed at the spiral groove.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Clinical examination is the **gold standard**.

elim: No fracture history; imaging does not confirm a nerve palsy.
A C7 root lesion would also weaken triceps.
Kept for unclear or non-recovering lesions; early studies may be normal.
Tests muscle damage, not nerve compression.

steps.x: **A. Clinical examination alone.** Nerve palsy: clinical examination first; NCS only if needed.

technique.stem: A 31 year old woman who is 32 weeks pregnant has 6 weeks of tingling in her right thumb, index and middle fingers that wakes her at night. Phalen's test is positive. There is no thenar wasting and thumb abduction power is normal. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Nerve conduction studies and await delivery

steps.x: Initial management: conservative before surgical.
**Mild carpal tunnel syndrome** in pregnancy, no wasting.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Wrist splint** (± steroid injection); it often settles after delivery.

elim: Surgery is for severe or refractory disease.
Clinical diagnosis; she needs symptom relief now.
Not first-line; local steroid injection is the option.

steps.x: **E. Wrist splint.** Mild CTS: splint ± steroid injection first.

technique.stem: A 16 year old boy has progressive bilateral foot drop, high-arched feet, distal leg wasting and reduced sensation in both feet. His father and paternal grandmother have the same problem. Genetic testing shows a PMP22 duplication.
technique.q: Which is the mode of inheritance?

steps.x: Inheritance question: read the pedigree in the stem.
Affected in every generation, both sexes, passed father to son: **Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT1A)**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Autosomal dominant**.

elim: Fathers cannot pass X-linked traits to sons.

steps.x: **A. Autosomal dominant.** CMT = autosomal dominant, most common hereditary neuropathy.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man woke on a friend's sofa with his right arm hung over the armrest after drinking heavily. He cannot extend his right wrist or fingers. Elbow extension is normal. Sensation is reduced over the dorsum of the first web space. His pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Radial nerve palsy at the spiral groove
practice.e: Saturday night palsy compresses the radial nerve at the spiral groove, giving wrist drop and dorsal first web space numbness with triceps spared. PIN palsy spares sensation.

steps.x: Diagnosis: nerve and level.

clues: cannot extend his right wrist or fingers
dorsum of the first web space
steps.x: Compression in the mid-arm while intoxicated, **wrist drop**, triceps spared, radial sensory loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Saturday night palsy**: radial nerve at the spiral groove.

elim: Would weaken triceps and reduce the triceps reflex.
Median: thenar weakness and lateral palmar fingers.

steps.x: **D. Radial nerve palsy at the spiral groove.** Wrist drop + web-space numbness + normal triceps = radial at spiral groove.

practice.stem: A 54 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has 4 months of numbness of her left thumb, index and middle fingers, worse at night. Tapping over the front of her wrist reproduces the tingling. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Claw hand of the 4th and 5th fingers
practice.e: Carpal tunnel syndrome compresses the median nerve at the wrist, weakening abductor pollicis brevis. Hypothenar wasting and clawing are ulnar.

steps.x: A finding question: name the diagnosis, then its sign.

clues: Tapping over the front of her wrist
steps.x: Positive **Tinel's**, median distribution, RA: **carpal tunnel syndrome**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Weak **abductor pollicis brevis**: weak thumb abduction, thenar wasting.
**C. Weak thumb abduction.** Carpal tunnel = weak APB, thenar wasting.

practice.stem: A 35 year old man had a fracture of the left fibular head in a football tackle 2 weeks ago. He now trips over his left foot. He cannot dorsiflex or evert the left ankle, but inversion is normal. Sensation is reduced over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which nerve is most likely injured?
practice.e: The common peroneal nerve wraps around the fibular neck; injury gives foot drop with weak eversion but normal inversion. Loss of inversion too suggests an L5 root lesion.

steps.x: Which nerve: use the mechanism and which ankle movements are spared.

clues: fracture of the left fibular head
steps.x: Fibular head fracture, foot drop, weak eversion, **inversion spared**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Common peroneal (fibular) nerve** palsy.

elim: Weak knee extension and anterior thigh numbness.
Would also weaken knee flexion and plantarflexion.

steps.x: **A. Common peroneal nerve.** Foot drop + eversion lost + inversion spared = common peroneal.

practice.stem: A newborn boy is noted to hold his right arm adducted and internally rotated with the elbow extended and the wrist flexed. Delivery was complicated by shoulder dystocia. He moves his right hand fingers normally. His pulse rate is 140 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Erb's palsy (C5/C6 upper trunk) gives the waiter's tip posture. Klumpke's (C8/T1) paralyses the small hand muscles, which are normal here.

steps.x: Diagnosis: a birth injury with a named posture.

clues: moves his right hand fingers normally
steps.x: **Waiter's tip** posture after shoulder dystocia with hand spared: upper trunk (C5/C6).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Erb's palsy**.

elim: Isolated deltoid weakness, not this posture.
Pseudoparalysis from pain, without the fixed posture.
C8/T1: paralysed small hand muscles, possible Horner's.

steps.x: **B. Erb's palsy.** Waiter's tip = Erb's (C5/C6).

practice.stem: A 49 year old woman has a sudden severe headache and drooping of her left eyelid. Her left eye is turned down and out and the left pupil is dilated and unreactive. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 168/96 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her nerve palsy?
practice.e: A surgical third nerve palsy (painful, dilated pupil) is most commonly due to a posterior communicating artery aneurysm. Diabetes causes a pupil-sparing palsy.

steps.x: A cause question: surgical or medical third nerve palsy?
Painful **third nerve palsy** with a **dilated pupil**: compression of the outer pupillary fibres.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Posterior communicating artery aneurysm**.
**D. Posterior communicating artery aneurysm.** Painful third nerve palsy + dilated pupil = PComm aneurysm.

practice.stem: A 42 year old man had diarrhoea 2 weeks ago. He now has double vision, an unsteady gait and falls. He cannot move his eyes fully in any direction, reflexes are absent and Romberg's test is positive. Limb power is normal. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 122/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Miller Fisher syndrome is the GBS variant with ataxia, areflexia and ophthalmoplegia, often after Campylobacter. The CSF shows a raised protein with normal cells.

steps.x: Diagnosis: find the triad.
**Ataxia, areflexia, ophthalmoplegia** after gastroenteritis (*Campylobacter*).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Miller Fisher syndrome**, a GBS variant.

elim: Descending paralysis with dilated pupils, from food or wounds.
Confusion and alcohol excess; reflexes not lost.

steps.x: **B. Miller Fisher syndrome.** Ataxia + areflexia + ophthalmoplegia = Miller Fisher.

practice.stem: A 46 year old woman has 6 months of numbness in her right hand. She cannot say which fingers are affected. Tinel's and Phalen's tests are equivocal and there is mild weakness of thumb abduction. Her GP is unsure whether this is carpal tunnel syndrome or a C6 radiculopathy.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to localise the lesion?
practice.e: When examination cannot localise the lesion, nerve conduction studies and EMG confirm and localise it (median slowing at the wrist versus a root lesion).

steps.x: Investigation to localise: the site is unclear.

clues: unsure whether this is carpal tunnel syndrome or a C6 radiculopathy
steps.x: Examination has not localised it: wrist or neck?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Nerve conduction studies/EMG** to confirm and localise.

elim: Screens for polyneuropathy, not a focal lesion.

steps.x: **C. Nerve conduction studies.** Clinical exam first; NCS/EMG if the site is unclear.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man has 5 days of tingling feet and weakness spreading up both legs and now into his arms, 3 weeks after a diarrhoeal illness. Reflexes are absent. He is admitted. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 132/84 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to monitor for respiratory failure?
practice.e: GBS is monitored with serial forced vital capacity because oxygen saturation and blood gases deteriorate late. The isolated CSF protein rise supports the diagnosis.

steps.x: Monitoring question: which test shows neuromuscular respiratory weakness early?
Ascending weakness, areflexia, post-infectious: **Guillain-Barré syndrome**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Serial **FVC**.

elim: Does not measure respiratory muscle strength.
Used for asthma, not for respiratory muscle weakness.

steps.x: **C. Forced vital capacity.** GBS: monitor with FVC.

practice.stem: A 63 year old woman has carpal tunnel syndrome confirmed on nerve conduction studies. She has worn a wrist splint and had a steroid injection over 6 months. She now has constant numbness and wasting of the thenar eminence. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: Severe or refractory carpal tunnel syndrome, especially with thenar wasting, is treated surgically by dividing the flexor retinaculum.

steps.x: Next step after conservative treatment has failed.

clues: wrist splint and had a steroid injection
steps.x: Severe CTS (wasting), failed **conservative** treatment.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Surgical division of the flexor retinaculum**.

elim: Wasting means conservative treatment has failed.
For ulnar nerve at the elbow.

steps.x: **B. Division of the flexor retinaculum.** Failed splint/injection or wasting = carpal tunnel release.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman has a 6 day history of ascending leg weakness and numbness after a chest infection. She now struggles to walk. Reflexes are absent. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Guillain-Barré syndrome is treated with IV immunoglobulin plus supportive care; corticosteroids are not effective.

steps.x: Initial management: name the condition, then its first-line drug.
Post-infectious ascending weakness with areflexia: **Guillain-Barré syndrome**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV immunoglobulin** plus supportive care.

elim: Supportive only; she cannot walk, so needs IVIG.

steps.x: **A. Intravenous immunoglobulin.** GBS = IVIG first-line.

practice.stem: A 22 year old man has a displaced mid-shaft fracture of the right humerus after a fall. He cannot extend his right wrist. His right hand is pale and cold, and the radial pulse cannot be felt. His pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Review in fracture clinic in 1 week
Urgent neurovascular assessment and orthopaedic review
practice.e: A nerve injury with a fracture needs urgent neurovascular assessment; a cold pulseless hand is a limb-threatening emergency before any splint or physiotherapy.

steps.x: Initial management with a threatened limb.
Radial nerve palsy **plus vascular compromise** after a fracture.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urgent **neurovascular** assessment and orthopaedic review.

elim: Not an emergency test and not useful early.
Later, after the fracture is managed.

steps.x: **E. Urgent neurovascular assessment and orthopaedic review.** Nerve injury with trauma = assess neurovascular status urgently.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman has had wrist drop for 3 days after sleeping with her arm over a chair. Nerve conduction studies show a conduction block at the spiral groove with normal amplitude below it. She recovers fully in 6 weeks. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her weakness?
practice.e: Compression causes focal demyelination and ischaemia, a conduction block without axon loss (neurapraxia), so recovery is rapid and complete.

steps.x: A mechanism question about a compression palsy.

clues: sleeping with her arm over a chair
steps.x: Compression, conduction block, axons intact, quick recovery: **neurapraxia**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Focal demyelination and ischaemia** blocking conduction.

elim: Neurotmesis does not recover without repair.

steps.x: **C. Focal demyelination and ischaemia.** Compression palsy = focal demyelination + ischaemia = neurapraxia.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the level decides wrist drop versus finger drop.

points.p: Mid-humeral shaft fracture (most common)

points.why: Extensors of wrist and fingers paralysed.

points.p: Elbow (radial head) level: finger drop with intact sensation
High axillary lesion (crutches): triceps weak too

points.p: Weak thumb abduction (APB)
Thenar wasting (not hypothenar)
Positive Tinel's and Phalen's
points.why: Tap test and wrist flexion test.

prompts.q: Ulnar nerve injury: hand signs, and what extra signs mean the lesion is at the elbow?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: FCU loss localises to the elbow.

points.p: Claw hand of 4th and 5th digits
Weak finger abduction and adduction
Radial deviation on wrist flexion (lost FCU)

prompts.q: Foot drop: how do you tell common peroneal palsy from L5 radiculopathy?

points.p: Common peroneal: weak dorsiflexion and eversion, inversion spared
Cause: fibular head fracture or knee dislocation

prompts.q: Other palsies: third nerve, long thoracic, suprascapular, axillary. Key features?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one sign per nerve.

points.p: Long thoracic: scapular winging
Suprascapular: cannot initiate abduction, weak Jobe's test

prompts.q: Miller Fisher, GBS, Charcot-Marie-Tooth and meralgia paraesthetica: one-line features?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: where it starts and what is inherited.

GBS: starts distally and ascends; isolated CSF protein rise; facial diplegia possible

Meralgia paraesthetica: burning lateral thigh, rapid weight gain

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: emergency first, then conservative before surgery.

points.p: Urgent neurovascular assessment with a fracture
points.why: A pulseless limb is an emergency.

points.p: Treat the cause: fracture, remove compression, adjust cast
Splint and physiotherapy; surgery if needed

points.why: Pregnancy CTS often settles after delivery.

prompts.q: What is the Seddon classification and what does each grade mean for prognosis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the more is cut, the worse it is.

points.p: Neurapraxia: temporary conduction block, best prognosis
points.why: Compression palsies: focal demyelination and ischaemia.

glossary.neurapraxia: Temporary nerve conduction block without axon damage; full recovery expected.
glossary.axonotmesis: Axon disrupted but its connective tissue sheath intact, so it can regrow.
glossary.neurotmesis: Complete cutting of a nerve; needs surgical repair.
glossary.Seddon classification: Grades nerve injury as neurapraxia, axonotmesis or neurotmesis.
glossary.endoneurium: Connective tissue around each nerve fibre that guides regrowth.
glossary.wrist drop: Inability to extend the wrist, from radial nerve injury.
glossary.finger drop: Inability to extend the fingers with the wrist spared, from posterior interosseous nerve injury.
glossary.spiral groove: Groove on the back of the humerus where the radial nerve runs.
glossary.Saturday night palsy: Radial nerve compression in the upper arm from sleeping on it while intoxicated.
glossary.posterior interosseous nerve: Motor branch of the radial nerve in the forearm; injury causes finger drop.
glossary.carpal tunnel syndrome: Median nerve compression at the wrist under the flexor retinaculum.
glossary.flexor retinaculum: Fibrous band forming the roof of the carpal tunnel; divided in surgery.
glossary.APB: Abductor pollicis brevis: thenar muscle that abducts the thumb, supplied by the median nerve.
glossary.thenar: The muscle bulge at the base of the thumb.
glossary.hypothenar: The muscle bulge at the base of the little finger.
glossary.Tinel's: Tapping over a nerve reproduces tingling in its territory.
glossary.Phalen's: Holding the wrists flexed for a minute reproduces carpal tunnel symptoms.
glossary.claw hand: Hyperextended knuckles with flexed fingers from weak hand intrinsics, typically ulnar.
glossary.FCU: Flexor carpi ulnaris: ulnar-supplied wrist flexor; loss makes the wrist deviate radially.
glossary.common peroneal nerve: Branch of the sciatic nerve wrapping round the fibular neck; supplies dorsiflexors and evertors.
glossary.deep peroneal: Branch of the common peroneal nerve supplying dorsiflexors and the first web space.
glossary.foot drop: Inability to dorsiflex the ankle, giving a high-stepping gait.
glossary.high-stepping gait: Lifting the knee high to clear a dropped foot.
glossary.Erb's palsy: C5/C6 brachial plexus injury giving the waiter's tip posture.
glossary.waiter's tip: Arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, wrist flexed: Erb's palsy.
glossary.Klumpke's palsy: C8/T1 brachial plexus injury paralysing the small hand muscles, possibly with Horner's.
glossary.Horner's: Ptosis, small pupil and reduced sweating from sympathetic chain damage.
glossary.shoulder dystocia: Baby's shoulder stuck behind the pelvis during delivery; can stretch the brachial plexus.
glossary.oculomotor: Third cranial nerve: moves most eye muscles, lifts the lid and constricts the pupil.
glossary.PComm: Posterior communicating artery; an aneurysm here compresses the third nerve.
glossary.pupil-sparing: Third nerve palsy with a normal pupil, typical of diabetic microvascular causes.
glossary.long thoracic nerve: Supplies serratus anterior; injury causes scapular winging.
glossary.scapular winging: Medial border of the scapula lifting off the chest wall.
glossary.Jobe's: Empty can test of supraspinatus strength.
glossary.axillary nerve: Supplies deltoid and skin over the lower lateral deltoid.
glossary.Miller Fisher syndrome: GBS variant with ataxia, areflexia and ophthalmoplegia.
glossary.ophthalmoplegia: Paralysis of the eye movement muscles.
glossary.Romberg's: Unsteadiness with eyes closed, showing loss of position sense.
glossary.GBS: Guillain-Barré syndrome: acute post-infectious ascending demyelinating polyneuropathy.
glossary.Campylobacter jejuni: Gut bacterium whose infection commonly triggers GBS.
glossary.molecular mimicry: Antibodies against a microbe cross-reacting with similar host proteins.
glossary.gangliosides: Glycolipids on nerve membranes targeted by antibodies in GBS.
glossary.FVC: Forced vital capacity; falls as respiratory muscles weaken in GBS.
glossary.IVIG: Intravenous immunoglobulin: pooled antibodies used to treat GBS.
glossary.Charcot-Marie-Tooth: Autosomal dominant inherited neuropathy with distal weakness and foot drop.
glossary.PMP22: Peripheral myelin protein 22; its duplication causes CMT1A.
glossary.meralgia paraesthetica: Compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh giving burning lateral thigh pain.
glossary.NCS: Nerve conduction studies: measure speed and size of nerve signals.
glossary.EMG: Electromyography: records muscle electrical activity to detect denervation.
glossary.MRC: Medical Research Council 0 to 5 scale for muscle power.
glossary.neurovascular: Relating to both nerves and blood vessels; checked after any limb injury.
